tutor.text: Which part of differentiation should we focus on today?

student.text: I know the rules, but worded questions trip me up.

tutor.text: At the highest point, is the ball's acceleration zero?

student.text: Yes, because it stops for a moment before falling.

tutor.text: Start with the units. What does moles per litre tell you?

student.text: Divide moles by volume. But do I convert millilitres first?

tutor.text: The magnetic force changes direction, not the particle's speed.

student.text: Oh, so it can accelerate without getting any faster!

tutor.text: Would a diagram or a verbal explanation help here?

student.text: Could we draw it? I'm losing track of the stages.

tutor.text: Now try differentiating x cubed without any hints.

student.text: Three x squared. Multiply by the power, then subtract one.

tutor.text: Your calculation is right. What is missing from the final answer?

student.text: The units. It should be moles per litre.

tutor.text: Before next time, trace binary search on two sorted lists.

student.text: I'll write down the midpoint and bounds at each step.

tutor.text: Why do we add a constant after indefinite integration?

student.text: Different constants give the same derivative.

tutor.text: Can you combine these logarithms before solving?

student.text: I added the arguments. Wait, I should multiply them.

tutor.text: What would one counterexample tell us about this claim?

student.text: That it is false, even if lots of examples work.

tutor.text: What changes when we know the first card was a king?

student.text: There are three kings left, out of fifty-one cards.

tutor.text: What does the area under a velocity-time graph give us?

student.text: Displacement. The units become metres.

tutor.text: How does the current split at this junction?

student.text: It splits equally, even if the resistances differ.

tutor.text: Choose a positive direction before writing the forces.

student.text: Then the weight is negative in my equation.

tutor.text: Which step still feels uncertain after that example?

student.text: Choosing the equation. I can do the algebra after that.

tutor.text: Does a catalyst change the equilibrium position?

student.text: Yes, it makes more product by speeding up the reaction.

tutor.text: What must you include when describing ionic bonding?

student.text: The attraction between oppositely charged ions.

tutor.text: What observation tells you the titration has reached its endpoint?

student.text: A colour change that stays after swirling.

tutor.text: What will you practise before our next organic lesson?

student.text: Reagents and conditions. I keep mixing those up.

tutor.text: Explain osmosis without using the word concentration.

student.text: Water moves from higher water potential to lower water potential.

tutor.text: Why does enzyme activity fall at very high temperatures?

student.text: The active site changes shape, so fewer substrates bind.

tutor.text: Does this correlation prove that the treatment caused the change?

student.text: No. Another variable might explain both results.

tutor.text: Can you recall the stages without looking at your notes?

student.text: Not yet. I recognise them, but cannot list them.

tutor.text: What happens if this recursive function has no base case?

student.text: It keeps calling itself until the stack runs out.

tutor.text: Try the empty list. What does your function return?

student.text: It crashes. I access the first item before checking.

tutor.text: If the input doubles, how many times does this loop run?

student.text: Twice as many. There is one pass through the list.

tutor.text: What makes this a testable requirement?

student.text: It needs a measurable result, not just easy to use.

tutor.text: What does multiplying by the imaginary unit do geometrically?

student.text: A quarter turn anticlockwise on the complex plane.

tutor.text: Would applying these two matrix transformations in reverse change the result?

student.text: I thought the order did not matter. Can we test it?

tutor.text: Which earlier method could help with this differential equation?

student.text: Separating the variables, if I can factor this first.

tutor.text: What part of the induction argument still needs work?

student.text: Showing the next case follows. I only checked the first.
